reviewed: branch codex/world-realistic-simulation-mvp at HEAD ebeacf9 (Re-freeze the runtime at the occupancy model).  Every demonstration below was run against a pristine 'git archive HEAD' checkout, because the working tree was being edited concurrently by another agent while this review ran; all line numbers refer to HEAD.  No repository file was modified by this review except this report.

findings.title: busy_until = start-of-act + lasts, so the WAIT before an act ('after') is counted as occupancy; a person is unavailable from now until the end of something they will do days later
findings.what_is_wrong: world_step computes due = now + after, then sets busy_until[doer] = due + lasts.  busy_until is a single 'free at' instant, so the whole interval [now, due) -- the WAIT before the act begins -- is treated as occupancy.  envelope.py:16-18 says 'lasts: how long it takes.  The person named in `by` is occupied for this long', and WORLD_SYSTEM (world_mind.py:185-190, 224-229) says "'after' is the wait before it starts", "'lasts' is how long it OCCUPIES the person doing it", and gives as its worked example "'after': 3 hours, 'lasts': a couple of minutes".  Code makes that three hours and a couple of minutes of being busy.  Consequences, all demonstrated: (1) an act the world says happens NOW is pushed to the end of an unrelated future act (waited_until_free); (2) the person is still_mid_task for the whole wait and is not consulted; (3) the push can carry the act past the cutoff, where it is DELETED (event_beyond_cutoff) and its deletion then sets intends_after_cutoff, which is what licenses NO_AT_CUTOFF.  In the second script Ada's reply -- which the world adjudicated as happening immediately, one hour into a fourteen-day window -- is destroyed and the run answers NO_AT_CUTOFF.
findings.smallest_fix: Occupancy must start when the act starts, not now: keep an interval rather than a single instant, or at minimum set busy_until[doer] = max(busy_until.get(doer, due), due + span) only for the span itself and clamp a later act with `due < busy_start or due < busy_end` semantics.  Concretely: record busy[doer] = (due, due + lasts) and, when scheduling the next act, push due to busy_end only if the proposed due falls INSIDE [busy_start, busy_end).  An act two days away must not make anybody busy today.

findings.title: The own_act_finished wake landing past the cutoff sets intends_after_cutoff, so a run whose queue simply ran dry is reported as the horizon honestly reached and answers NO_AT_CUTOFF
findings.what_is_wrong: When an act is scheduled, code schedules a wake at due + lasts.  If that instant is past the cutoff, _schedule_wake takes the 'beyond the deadline' branch and sets intends_after_cutoff['yes'] = True.  reached_horizon is then True at line 1050 and finish('') advances the clock across the whole unlived remainder and judges final=True, which is the only place NO_AT_CUTOFF is reachable.  But 'this act finishes after the deadline' is not the evidence intends_after_cutoff is supposed to carry: the comment at 226 and at 526-536 says it means 'somebody's own stated next move lies past the deadline' / 'the world has said what happens next and none of it lands inside the window'.  Here something DID land inside the window; only its duration spills over.  The demonstration runs the identical world twice, changing one string -- lasts '10 minutes' vs '20 days' -- and the run flips from incomplete_empty_queue/UNRESOLVED to cutoff/NO_AT_CUTOFF, with two committed events either way and thirteen unlived days.  This is the same defect the repo's own test_whether_a_no_is_reachable_does_not_depend_on_arithmetic exists to prevent, with `lasts` in place of the wake interval, and it re-opens the failure class the branch was created to close ('eleven of eleven NO answers stopped because the queue emptied').

"""F1: an act whose `lasts` runs past the cutoff sets intends_after_cutoff,
turning an unlived (incomplete_empty_queue) window into an authoritative NO."""
import json, sys
sys.path.insert(0, "tests")

from sworldmodel.semantic_runtime.llm import RuntimeCaller
from sworldmodel.semantic_runtime.trace import Trace
from sworldmodel.semantic_runtime.trajectory import run_trajectory
from test_semantic_runtime import (CUTOFF, FINAL_MARKER, NO_AT_CUTOFF, NOTHING,
                                   SCENE, START, UNRESOLVED, build, reviewed)


def terminal_roles(user, system):
    if "read-only outcome judge" in system \
            or "whether a stated condition has been met" in system:
        return json.dumps(NO_AT_CUTOFF if FINAL_MARKER in user
                          else UNRESOLVED), {}
    return None


def make_world(lasts):
    """One act at the start, then total silence.  The ONLY difference
    between the two runs is how long that one act takes."""
    n = {"i": 0}

    def transport(system, user):
        t = terminal_roles(user, system)
        if t:
            return t
        if "You are the world" in system:
            if "starting_event" in user and n["i"] == 0:
                n["i"] = 1
                return json.dumps({
                    "judgment": "she settles in to it.",
                    "event": {"description": "Ada begins reading the file.",
                              "for": ["ada_vance"], "observed": True,
                              "after": "0 seconds", "by": "ada_vance",
                              "lasts": lasts},
                    "wakes": []}), {}
            return json.dumps({"judgment": "nothing follows.",
                               "event": None, "wakes": []}), {}
        return json.dumps(NOTHING), {}
    return transport


for lasts in ("10 minutes", "20 days"):
    world, journal, bindings = build()
    trace = Trace()
    caller = RuntimeCaller(transport=reviewed(make_world(lasts)))
    traj = run_trajectory(world, journal, bindings, SCENE["resolution"],
                          caller, max_steps=40, trace=trace)
    print(f"lasts={lasts!r:14} -> status={traj.status:24} "
          f"answer={(traj.answer or {}).get('status')}")
    for w in trace.of("wake_beyond_cutoff"):
        print(f"     wake_beyond_cutoff: provenance={w['provenance']!r} "
              f"due={w['due']} actor={w['actor']}")
    print(f"     events committed={len(journal.events())}")
    print(f"     final clock={world.clock.now.isoformat()}  cutoff={CUTOFF}")

findings.title: The new same-doer/same-audience duplicate rule has no time bound and no verb: it deletes a chase four days later, and it merges an acceptance with a refusal
findings.what_is_wrong: `already_committed` is built from EVERY committed event of the run plus everything pending (trajectory.py:349-355), so the comparison has no temporal scope at all.  _shape() sorts a SET of tokens, so word order, the verb's subject and negation are all destroyed; only _facts (digits, one..ten, and capitalised words of >=3 letters) survives.  Two consequences.  (a) OVER-MERGE OF A GENUINE REPEAT: a follow-up is a different act at a different time, and the continuity reviewer was JUST changed to say so ('CHASING IS NOT A DEFECT ... ringing back, asking a second time, sending another message', actor_mind.py:253-257).  The world-side dedup deletes it anyway: 'Ada sends Bo another message asking him to confirm the hall' vs 'Ada sends Bo a message asking him to confirm the hall' scores 0.918 and is dropped four days later, so the chase never happens.  The two changes in this commit range cancel each other out.  (b) OVER-MERGE OF OPPOSITES: negation is invisible to a bag of words.  'Ada replies that she accepts the offer' / '... does not accept the offer' = 0.872; 'Ada tells Bo she can host on Saturday' / '... cannot host ...' = 0.959; 'Ada confirms the booking is going ahead' / '... is not going ahead' = 0.947.  All three are same-doer, same-audience pairs a negotiation produces routinely, all three merge, and in each the DECISIVE act is the one deleted.  Lowering SAME_ACT from 0.86 to 0.80 widened this; at 0.86 the accepts/does-not-accept pair still merges.

"""F3: pairs the new same-doer/same-audience dedup MERGES that are
genuinely different acts, and repeats it still misses."""
import difflib
from sworldmodel.semantic_runtime.world_mind import (says_the_same_thing,
                                                     _facts, _shape, SAME_ACT)

OVER = [
 # acceptance vs refusal -- opposite outcomes of the same negotiation
 ("Ada replies that she accepts the offer.",
  "Ada replies that she does not accept the offer."),
 ("Ada tells Bo she can host on Saturday.",
  "Ada tells Bo she cannot host on Saturday."),
 ("Ada confirms the booking is going ahead.",
  "Ada confirms the booking is not going ahead."),
 # opposite direction of the same transaction
 ("Ada sends Bo the signed contract.",
  "Bo sends Ada the signed contract."),          # (differs only in by/for)
 ("Ada pays Bo the deposit.", "Ada pays Bo the balance."),
 # a promise vs its fulfilment
 ("Ada says she will send the report.", "Ada sends the report."),
 # different objects of the same verb
 ("Ada emails the landlord about the boiler.",
  "Ada emails the landlord about the rent."),
 ("Ada cancels the Tuesday viewing.", "Ada cancels the viewing."),
 # a chase: the same act done a second time, days later, is a real act
 ("Ada sends Bo a message asking him to confirm the hall.",
  "Ada sends Bo another message asking him to confirm the hall."),
 ("Ada rings Bo and leaves a voicemail.",
  "Ada rings Bo again and leaves a second voicemail."),
]
MISS = [
 ("Ada signs the lease.", "Ada signs the lease."),   # same, order of `for`
]

print(f"threshold SAME_ACT={SAME_ACT}\n")
print("=== pairs the rule MERGES (the later one is DELETED) ===")
for a, b in OVER:
    r = difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, _shape(a), _shape(b)).ratio()
    same = says_the_same_thing(a, b)
    print(f"{'MERGED ' if same else 'kept   '} ratio={r:.3f}  facts_equal="
          f"{_facts(a)==_facts(b)}\n    A: {a}\n    B: {b}")

findings.smallest_fix: Two independent changes.  (1) Bound the comparison in time: only compare against events committed or pending at the SAME instant (or within one MIN_STEP), which is the loop the rule was written for ('she reads the next portion of the results section' nine times), and is never a legitimate repeat.  (2) Make negation and polarity part of _facts: reject any pair whose sets of {not, cannot, n't, no, never, declines, refuses, accepts, agrees} differ, the same way differing numbers already disqualify a match.

findings.title: `by: null` is accepted on an actor_intention adjudication, so the whole occupancy model is optional and two of one person's acts overlap
findings.what_is_wrong: Everything occupancy does is keyed on envelope['by'] (the waited_until_free clamp, busy_until, the own_act_finished wake, and the still_mid_task guard).  validate_event permits by=null unconditionally and code never cross-checks it against the trigger, even though on an actor_intention turn the runtime itself stamps the event with self_act_of=actor_id and did_it=actor_id (lines 310, 318) and grants that actor observation of it 'because it was their own doing' (1135-1141).  So a single null makes the record say both 'nobody did this' and 'she knows she did it', and turns off one-thing-at-a-time.  The demonstration is the repo's own busy_world fixture with `by` changed to null: the second act begins 120s into a thirty-minute call instead of 1800s, and still_mid_task never fires.  journal.py:60-64 states the point exactly -- 'A ledger that cannot say a call took half an hour cannot be audited for whether anybody was in two places at once' -- and by=null is precisely the case where the ledger cannot say it.  The runtime's own test suite writes "by": None on actor_intention adjudications in four places, so this is not a hypothetical shape.
findings.smallest_fix: In world_step, when trigger_kind == 'actor_intention', reject by=None the same way a foreign `by` is rejected (or coerce doer = envelope['by'] or actor_id for the occupancy computation).  If the consequence really is environmental, self_act_of/did_it must be cleared too, so the record is consistent either way.

findings.title: The own_act_finished wake is placed at the end of the LAST-SCHEDULED act, and keep_latest lets a far-off act cancel the genuine 'you are free now' wake, stranding the person
findings.what_is_wrong: The wake is scheduled at due + lasts of whatever was scheduled most recently, with keep_latest=True so a later due always wins.  Because due includes `after` (see the first finding), an act two days away produces a wake two days away, which cancels the wake that was correctly sitting at the end of the thirty-minute call the person is actually on.  In the demonstration Ada rings Bo (30 minutes) and says she will post a letter on Wednesday; the 14:30 free-wake is cancelled in the ledger and replaced with one at 14:05 two days later, and she is still_mid_task and unconsulted for the whole interval.  _after_commit's comment (829-833) explicitly promises the opposite: 'They are brought back the moment it ends, by the wake scheduled where the occupancy was set -- so this costs nobody their turn'.  Secondary: the guard is `ends > world.clock.now`, not `lasts > 0`, so EVERY future-dated act of a person mints an own_act_finished wake for them even when lasts is '0 seconds' and nothing occupied them -- a poll, in a module whose header says 'There is no polling ... Time passing is not a reason to think about something again.'
findings.smallest_fix: Schedule the free-wake from the occupancy interval, not from the event: only when lasts > 0, at (due + lasts), and only if that is later than the person's current busy_until -- never cancelling a pending free-wake that falls before it.

findings.title: MAX_WORLD_RUN is disarmed: _hand_back_the_turn can only ever consult an actor who has NEVER been consulted, yet it zeroes since_actor unconditionally
findings.what_is_wrong: _has_learned_something(aid) is news[aid] > news_at_turn[aid]; every completed actor_step sets news_at_turn[aid] = news[aid] (line 632), and news[aid] is only ever incremented immediately before an actor_step for that same aid (757-760).  So after an actor's first turn the predicate is permanently False.  _hand_back_the_turn therefore consults nobody -- but its FIRST line is since_actor['n'] = 0, so the bound is rearmed for free and the world carries straight on.  The measured result: 54 consecutive world adjudications with not one person consulted, against MAX_WORLD_RUN=6; 41 committed events, 2 actor turns in the whole run, and the step ceiling reached.  That is the exact failure the constant was introduced for ('thirty-three consecutive events of one man typing, none of them his own model's doing, and the budget was gone before anyone was asked anything').  The docstring also claims it withholds the turn from 'someone in the middle of their own long task'; there is no busy check in the function at all.

findings.title: The 'restatement' rule deletes any event on the attention trigger that nobody in the cast did -- i.e. exactly the outside-party events the world prompt demands
findings.what_is_wrong: The guard drops a pending_progression event whenever by is null and the concerned actor is not among those who observed it.  Its comment says it only catches 'the item's own state narrated again', but the condition is purely 'no person in the cast did it and nobody noticed it yet', which is the shape of every real exogenous event: an agency withdrawing a property, an office closing, a third party cancelling, a machine breaking.  WORLD_SYSTEM (world_mind.py:134-141) instructs the world to produce exactly those on ANY trigger ('People and organisations OUTSIDE the list of actors act too -- they chase, they follow up, they close their books ... A situation in which the only thing that ever goes wrong is that somebody did not get round to it is not a realistic situation').  So the one thing the new elapsed_world turn was added to make possible is still deleted everywhere except on elapsed_world.  In the demonstration 'The letting agency withdraws the property from the market.' is refused.

findings.smallest_fix: Narrow the guard to what it claims to catch: refuse only when the proposed description is a near-restatement of one of the `concerns` items already in the record (reuse says_the_same_thing against the pending items), not merely because by is null.

findings.title: not_before is the previous event's START, and is applied regardless of who did either thing, so a second attempt the world says happens now is pushed to whenever the first begins
findings.what_is_wrong: floor = result['landed_at'] is the START instant of the previous attempt's event, and every later attempt in the turn is forced to due >= floor.  Nothing checks that the same person is doing both, or that the first act has finished, or that the world did not already answer with a deliberately different time.  So a person who states 'book the viewing' (world: in two days) and 'ring the office' (world: now) has the phone call moved two days.  The demonstration sets by=null on both events, so occupancy is provably not involved and the trace shows ordered_after_earlier_attempt doing it alone.  WORLD_SYSTEM (world_mind.py:197-200) tells the world 'you do not need to arrange that, the machinery does it.  Say how long each thing really takes and the order looks after itself' -- and the machinery then discards the times it just asked for.
findings.smallest_fix: Make the floor the previous event's END (landed_at + its lasts), and apply it only when the two events name the same doer -- which is what occupancy already does correctly.  A second attempt whose consequence is environmental, or belongs to a later moment the world chose, must keep the world's time.

findings.title: The world's own turn is never taken for the jump from where the loop stopped to the cutoff -- usually the longest unlived stretch in the run
findings.file: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:997-1052 (the `ev is None or ev.t > cutoff` branch precedes the elapsed_world gate at 1080) and 943-951 (finish)
findings.what_is_wrong: UNLIVED_TIME_WORTH_ASKING_ABOUT is described as 'How much unlived time has to lie ahead before code asks the world what happened in it', but the gate at 1080 is only reached when there IS a next event inside the window. The demonstration lives 1 event across a fourteen-day window, takes zero elapsed_world turns, and answers NO_AT_CUTOFF -- structurally the same 'a cold email jumped its whole fortnight in one record' shape the branch exists to remove, now blessed as an honest horizon.

findings.title: The world's own turn is asked 'what happens between now and T?' and nothing makes the answer land before T
findings.what_is_wrong: The trigger text names the window explicitly, but the returned event is scheduled at now + after like any other, with no upper bound. findings.title: replay._projection builds every actor view without busy_until, so the section of the prompt an actor was actually handed is outside everything `exact` checks -- and it is not derivable from the ledger
findings.what_is_wrong: build_view(world, journal, aid) is called with no busy_until on both sides of the comparison, so views['<aid>']['busy_until'] is always None and views_match is a comparison of two identically degraded projections.  The demonstration shows a live run in which Ada was handed a view carrying 'You are occupied until 2026-07-30T14:00:00+00:00' while the replay projection reconstructs None for the same actor, and exact is still True.  Worse, busy_until is not reconstructible from the ledger even in principle: it is written at SCHEDULE time (trajectory.py:511) from events that may never commit -- a run that breaks with events still queued leaves occupancy state with no ledger counterpart, so World.from_records(live=True) would resume with different occupancy from the live run.  The claim 'replaying its records reconstructs the world without any model being consulted' is now true only of the parts occupancy does not touch.

findings.title: An arrival is recorded as already-asked BEFORE the MAX_WORLD_RUN break, so for the second recipient the question is booked as put and never put
findings.what_is_wrong: The loop writes arrivals_asked[(aid, event_id)] = True and only then tests `if since_actor['n'] >= MAX_WORLD_RUN: break`.  Each world_step in the loop increments since_actor, so with two or more unseen recipients the counter can cross the threshold between iterations: the next recipient is marked asked, the loop breaks, and because arrivals_asked is a permanent latch the world is never asked what becomes of that item for that person -- for that item, ever.  The guard at 770-773 returns before the loop whenever since_actor is already at the threshold, so this is reachable only in the narrow window since_actor == MAX_WORLD_RUN - 1 on entry, which is why I could not exhibit it: in the multi-recipient run I built, the earlier guard fired first every time and the two recipients were asked equally often (23 and 23).  The mark-before-ask ordering is plainly wrong regardless.
findings.demonstration: SPECULATIVE.  Reasoning above; the ordering is visible directly at trajectory.py:795-800 (mark at 797, break at 798-799, ask at 800-806).  My attempt to exhibit it is f10_arrival_marked_but_never_asked.py, which shows 30 two-recipient unobserved items and 23 arrival questions per person -- the seven missing ones are the 770-773 early return, not this break, so it does not prove the point.
findings.smallest_fix: Move the arrivals_asked assignment to after the break, immediately before world_step.

checked_and_clean: busy_until never shrinks.  due is clamped UP to busy_until before use (trajectory.py:472-476) and ends = due + lasts, so every assignment is >= the previous value; the beyond-cutoff branch leaves it untouched.  An auditor over five scripted runs found no pair of committed events with the same non-null `by` whose [t, t+lasts) intervals overlap.

The free-wake is never duplicated.  pending_wakes is keyed (actor, provenance), popped when the wake fires, and the previous one is cancelled through the ledger before a replacement is pushed; the queue refuses duplicate seqs.  I could not produce two live own_act_finished wakes for one actor.

No non-terminating run found.  Adversarial worlds -- zero-delay events, `by` alternating between actors to force identity hand-backs on every adjudication, three intentions every turn, wakes at every opportunity -- both terminated on the step ceiling well inside a 90s alarm (f12_hang_probe.py).  The two `continue` paths that do not increment traj.steps (the empty-queue sweep and elapsed_world) are each latched on world.clock.now, which is monotonic.

Mutual actor<->actor recursion through the identity guard terminates: actor_step writes news_at_turn[actor] BEFORE dispatching its intentions (line 632), so a re-entrant consultation of the same actor at the same instant hits the guard at 568-570 and returns.

The identity guard does cover elapsed_world.  adjudicating_for is None on that turn and the `or trigger_kind == 'elapsed_world'` clause at 416 picks it up; a named `by` is handed back, nothing is committed, and the world call is still recorded.

Ledger integrity and exact replay hold on every scenario I built, including runs containing cancelled wakes, dropped duplicates, dropped beyond-cutoff events, a step-limit truncation and a 41-event world monologue: exact=True, ledger_integrity=[] in all of them (f9_audit.py).

No record moves time backwards and no committed event precedes the timestamp of its cause, in any scenario (checked record by record in f9_audit.py).  world.schedule would raise SchedulingInPastError anyway, and every due is computed as now + a non-negative delta and only ever moved forward.
The clock is never advanced without a record: advance_to(ev.t) is followed by event.fired, and advance_to(cutoff) by OP_HORIZON.

'WHAT YOU ARE IN THE MIDDLE OF RIGHT NOW' is genuinely reachable from a run, not only from the hand-built view in the test: a world_process wake landing inside an occupied interval produces it (f15_busy_section_never_shown.py, 1 of 6 views in each of three scenarios).

elapsed_world is asked at most once per instant and does not spin: asked_about_the_gap is set before the call and compared against world.clock.now, and a null answer falls through to the pop on the next iteration.
